temperature.name: Temperature
temperature.description: Temperature describes how warm or cold the air is. Humidity, air movement, clothing, and activity also affect how it feels. The project combines these conditions in PMV to describe seven thermal sensations; it does not rate air temperature alone.
temperature.advice: If you feel cold or warm, try a small change to clothing, air conditioning, or a fan, then give it time. Comfort varies, so there is no need to keep adjusting just to reach Neutral.

pmv.name: PMV thermal sensation
pmv.description: PMV estimates a group’s average thermal sensation from air and radiant temperature, humidity, air speed, activity, and clothing. Negative values indicate cooler sensations, positive values warmer ones, and values near zero neutral sensations. Individual feelings can still differ.
pmv.advice: If you feel cold or warm, try a small change to clothing, air conditioning, or a fan, then give it time. Comfort varies, so there is no need to keep adjusting just to reach Neutral.

cold.label: Cold
cold.detail: The space feels cold. Consider more heating or warmer clothing.

cool.label: Cool
cool.detail: The space feels cool. Add clothing if needed.

slightly_cool.label: Slightly cool
slightly_cool.detail: It feels slightly cool. Clothing and activity may affect comfort.

neutral.label: Neutral
neutral.summary: Most people may find the temperature neutral.
neutral.detail: Most people may find the temperature neutral.

slightly_warm.label: Slightly warm
slightly_warm.detail: It feels slightly warm. Consider whether to lower the temperature.

warm.label: Warm
warm.detail: The space feels warm. Ventilation or lighter clothing may help.

hot.label: Hot
hot.detail: The space feels hot. Consider cooling it.

humidity.name: Relative humidity
humidity.description: Relative humidity is the percentage of water vapor in the air compared with saturation at the same temperature. Dry air may feel uncomfortable, while persistent dampness supports mold growth. Staying within the selected reference range helps balance comfort and moisture control.
humidity.advice: When air is dry, add moisture as needed. When damp, check bathrooms, drying laundry, or leaks, then consider exhaust ventilation or a dehumidifier. Opening windows may not help if outdoor air is also humid.

dry.label: Dry
dry.detail: The air is dry. Humidify if needed.

suitable.label: Suitable
suitable.summary: Humidity is within the selected reference range.
suitable.detail: Humidity is within the selected reference range.

slightly_humid.label: Slightly humid
slightly_humid.detail: Humidity is slightly high. Watch ventilation and condensation.

humid.label: Humid
humid.detail: Humidity is high. Consider ventilation or dehumidification.

co2.name: CO₂
co2.description: CO₂ can build up indoors as people breathe and helps indicate ventilation conditions. A sustained rise suggests a need for more fresh air. It does not represent every pollutant or replace a carbon monoxide alarm.
co2.advice: High CO₂ often points to insufficient ventilation. When outdoor air is suitable, open a window or bring in fresh air mechanically. Opening a door may help circulation, but fresh air still needs to enter. Pay closer attention when more people are present or windows stay closed.

good.label: Normal
good.detail: Ventilation looks good for now. Keep your usual fresh-air routine.

moderate.label: Ventilate
moderate.summary: Try opening a window or bringing in fresh air, then check whether the reading falls.
moderate.detail: Try opening a window or bringing in fresh air, then check whether the reading falls.

poor.label: Increase ventilation
poor.detail: Increase fresh-air supply soon. In a crowded room, spreading people out may also help.

pm25.name: PM2.5
pm25.description: PM2.5 is fine airborne particulate matter generally no more than 2.5 micrometers in aerodynamic diameter. Sources include combustion, cooking, and outdoor pollution. These particles can enter the lungs; consider concentration, duration, and outdoor conditions when reducing sources or filtering air.
pm25.advice: If readings rise after cooking, incense, or smoking, reduce the smoke source, use an extractor, or run particle filtration. Check outdoor air before opening windows; polluted air can bring more particles inside.

good.label: Good
good.detail: The concentration is low. Keep your current routine and check it from time to time.

fair.label: Fair
fair.detail: Above the lowest band. Check for an obvious source or a recent activity that may explain it.

moderate.detail: Pay a little more attention. Try the steps above and check the reading again.

very_poor.label: Very poor
very_poor.detail: The concentration is very high. Limit time in the affected area and check local guidance or investigate sources.

extremely_poor.label: Extremely poor
extremely_poor.summary: This is the highest rating band.
extremely_poor.detail: This is the highest rating band. Prioritize leaving the polluted area and follow relevant guidance.

pm10.name: PM10
pm10.description: PM10 is inhalable particulate matter generally no more than 10 micrometers in aerodynamic diameter, including PM2.5. Dust, roads, and construction can raise readings. Consider outdoor conditions when controlling dust and improving filtration.
pm10.advice: Cleaning, movement, or dusty weather can raise PM10. Damp wiping instead of dry sweeping can reduce dust. Check filtration, and limit open windows when outdoor dust is heavy.

hcho.name: Formaldehyde (HCHO)
hcho.description: Formaldehyde is a gas that may be released by panels, furniture, and other materials. Read concentrations over the averaging period required by the selected reference. If elevated, check emission sources and ventilate when outdoor conditions allow.
hcho.advice: New furniture or renovation materials may keep releasing formaldehyde. If elevated, look for sources and ventilate when outdoor air is suitable. Persistent readings may warrant professional testing. No noticeable smell does not prove levels have fallen.

tvoc.name: TVOC Index
tvoc.description: The TVOC index tracks changes in a sensor’s combined response to volatile organic compounds. It is not the concentration of one pollutant or a direct measure of toxicity or health risk. This project currently displays readings and trends without rating bands.

noise.name: Noise
noise.description: Noise readings describe sound level at the measurement location. A weighting reflects the ear’s differing sensitivity to frequencies. Effects on rest depend on duration and context; the sleep scene uses stricter boundaries.
noise.advice: If sound affects focus or rest, lower the volume, move noisy equipment, or find a quieter spot. Use the sleep scene for guidance when resting, as sound can be more disruptive then.

quiet.summary: Sound levels are low and suit quiet activities.
quiet.detail: Sound levels are low and suit quiet activities.

noticeable.detail: Sound is noticeable and may affect focus or rest.

loud.label: Loud
loud.detail: The space is loud. Try reducing noise at its source.

very_loud.label: Very loud
very_loud.detail: The space is very loud. Limit prolonged exposure.

illuminance.name: Light / Illuminance
illuminance.description: Illuminance measures visible light falling on a surface, in lux. Different activities need different levels; brighter is not always better. A single device reading is a scene hint. Check the actual task surface for reading or work.
illuminance.advice: For reading, writing, or crafts, add a light at the task location and adjust it to avoid hand shadows and glare. Light at the device may differ from the desk, so a higher number is not the goal by itself.

low_light.label: Low light
low_light.detail: This reading is low. Check illuminance at the activity location.

o3.name: Ozone O₃
o3.description: This is ground-level ozone, not the protective ozone layer high above Earth. It can form when other pollutants react in sunlight. At elevated levels, consult local forecasts to adjust outdoor activity timing and intensity.
o3.advice: When ozone is high, move strenuous outdoor activities such as running or cycling to a lower forecast period, or shorten them. Check outdoor ozone before opening windows; a fresh smell is not a reliable guide.

co.name: Carbon monoxide CO
co.description: Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas that can result from incomplete combustion. This rating uses outdoor air quality references and their averaging periods. Acute hazards require a dedicated alarm; do not wait for an air quality rating to rise.
co.advice: These bands describe outdoor air quality. If a CO alarm sounds or you suspect a combustion leak, leave the affected area immediately and seek local emergency help. Do not wait for a rating change or rely only on opening windows.

so2.name: Sulfur dioxide SO₂
so2.description: Sulfur dioxide is mainly associated with sulfur-containing fuel combustion and some industrial emissions, and can affect breathing. Interpret readings over the selected reference’s averaging period. At elevated levels, follow local guidance to reduce exposure.
so2.advice: When outdoor SO₂ is high, spend less time in affected places and move outdoor activities to a cleaner-air period. Consider outdoor readings before ventilating; opening windows may not help when levels are high.

pollen.name: Pollen
pollen.description: Pollen readings count grains per volume of air. Allergenic potential and rating thresholds differ by type and reference. Sensitive people can plan activities based on their own response. A total count without a type does not establish a load rating.
pollen.advice: If you are sensitive to pollen, read the count alongside your own reactions. When pollen is abundant, avoid leaving windows open for long and change outer clothing after going out. Different pollen types can affect you differently at the same count.

absent.label: Not detected
absent.summary: The measured pollen count is zero.
absent.detail: The measured pollen count is zero.

low.label: Low
low.summary: The load of this pollen type is low.
low.detail: The load of this pollen type is low.

high.detail: Pollen load is high. Sensitive people may wish to plan outdoor activities.

very_high.label: Extreme
very_high.detail: Pollen load is extreme. Sensitive people should consider protection.

uv_index.name: UV Index
uv_index.description: The UV Index describes the potential strength of solar UV damage to skin and eyes, not visible illuminance. Higher values call for greater attention to sun protection and shade. Distinguish a current reading from the daily maximum.
uv_index.advice: Check the UV Index before heading out and prepare a hat, covering clothing, or sunscreen. At higher levels, use shade and limit midday exposure. Cool or cloudy weather does not always mean low UV.

moderate.label: Moderate
moderate.detail: UV is moderate. Keep exposure time in mind.

high.label: High
high.detail: UV is high. Use sun protection outdoors.

very_high.label: Very high
very_high.detail: UV is very high. Limit midday exposure.

extreme.label: Extreme
extreme.detail: UV is extreme. Avoid unnecessary outdoor exposure.

iso_7730_2025.name: ISO 7730:2025
iso_7730_2025.description: ISO 7730 is an international standard for understanding how people experience the thermal environment. It looks beyond air temperature to humidity, air speed, radiant temperature, clothing, and activity. PMV and PPD estimate a group’s thermal sensation and the proportion likely to be dissatisfied; this project uses those methods to explain cooler, warmer, or near-neutral conditions.

ashrae_55_scale.name: ASHRAE Standard 55 seven-point scale
ashrae_55_scale.description: The seven-point thermal sensation scale used in ASHRAE Standard 55 describes sensations from Cold through Neutral to Hot, on a scale from −3 to +3. This gives a more familiar meaning to a PMV number. The project uses these names with its own continuous display bands; a label alone does not establish that a room meets the full standard.
ashrae_55_scale.organization: American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE)

epa_humidity.name: U.S. EPA humidity guidance
epa_humidity.description: The US EPA’s humidity guidance helps households manage dampness and mold. It recommends keeping indoor relative humidity around 30–50% where possible, and below 60%. The project offers this as an optional reference, using Dry, Suitable, Slightly Humid, and Humid messages to help you consider humidification, ventilation, or dehumidification.

uba_humidity.name: German UBA humidity guidance
uba_humidity.description: The German Environment Agency’s humidity guidance approaches moisture through everyday ventilation and damp prevention, suggesting roughly 40–60% relative humidity throughout the year. It provides a simple reference range for the home. This is the project’s default: readings below the range are Dry and those above it Humid, helping you decide whether to add or remove moisture.

eea_aqi.name: EEA European Air Quality Index
eea_aqi.description: The European Air Quality Index, provided by the European Environment Agency, translates pollutant concentrations into six easy-to-read levels for understanding short-term air conditions. It is the project’s default for PM2.5 and PM10, with corresponding ozone and sulfur dioxide bands also available. The displayed results describe individual pollutants, rather than a complete official European aggregate index.

hj_633_2026.name: HJ 633—2026
hj_633_2026.description: HJ 633—2026 sets out China’s technical rules for calculating AQI from pollutant concentrations, assigning pollution categories, and reporting results. The project uses its concentration boundaries for particulate matter and supported outdoor gases. Readings must also match the required averaging period: an hourly value and a daily average are not interchangeable.
hj_633_2026.organization: Ministry of Ecology and Environment of the People's Republic of China

epa_aqi.name: U.S. EPA AQI
epa_aqi.description: The US EPA AQI reports air quality in six categories to help people decide when to pay closer attention to pollution or adjust outdoor activities. The project offers its concentration boundaries for supported pollutants as an alternative reference. Averaging periods and numeric processing differ by pollutant, so the same reading may receive a different rating under another reference.

uba_co2_2008.name: German UBA 2008 CO₂ guidance
uba_co2_2008.description: The German Environment Agency’s CO₂ guidance helps identify indoor ventilation conditions that deserve attention. It uses 1000 and 2000 ppm as the boundaries between three ranges. The project turns these into Normal, Ventilate, and Increase Ventilation messages, helping you consider opening windows or adding fresh air. The reference does not assess other pollutants such as carbon monoxide.

who_hcho_2010.name: WHO 2010 Guidelines for Indoor Air Quality
who_hcho_2010.description: The WHO indoor air quality guidelines provide health-based references for several indoor pollutants. For formaldehyde, the reference is 0.10 mg/m³ over a 30-minute averaging period. This is the project’s default formaldehyde reference. The project builds six messages around that value; those six bands are a product presentation, not six categories prescribed by WHO.

gbt_18883_2022.name: GB/T 18883—2022
gbt_18883_2022.description: GB/T 18883—2022 is China’s indoor air quality standard, covering pollutant limits and test methods. Its formaldehyde limit is 0.08 mg/m³ as a one-hour average. The project offers it as an optional formaldehyde reference. Its six display bands are product rules based on that limit; the display is not a complete indoor air quality compliance test.
gbt_18883_2022.organization: State Administration for Market Regulation / Standardization Administration of China

oehha_hcho_2008.name: California OEHHA 2008
oehha_hcho_2008.description: California OEHHA publishes reference exposure levels to support assessment of health risks from air pollutants. Its one-hour acute reference value for formaldehyde is 0.055 mg/m³. The project offers this option for products using the California reference. It is not a nationwide US legal limit, and the six displayed bands are the project’s own mapping.
oehha_hcho_2008.organization: California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA)

who_noise_1999.name: WHO Guidelines for Community Noise
who_noise_1999.description: The WHO Guidelines for Community Noise consider how sound affects everyday life, rest, and sleep, and provide references for different settings. Relevant values use measures such as long-term equivalent sound levels. The project draws on home and sleep references for understandable noise messages. Its four bands for current sound readings are product rules and do not replace the guideline’s full long-term measurements.

ies_rp_11_26.name: ANSI/IES/ALA RP-11-26
ies_rp_11_26.description: ANSI/IES/ALA RP-11-26 is a recommended practice for indoor and outdoor residential lighting, with guidance for spaces, activities, and actual task surfaces. The project uses selected illuminance levels to describe activities from ambient lighting to detail work. This makes a reading easier to understand, while recognizing that one device location does not represent a desk surface or an entire room.
ies_rp_11_26.organization: Illuminating Engineering Society (IES) / American Lighting Association (ALA)

nab_pollen.name: NAB pollen levels
nab_pollen.description: The US National Allergy Bureau’s monitoring network describes pollen load using concentrations for categories such as trees, grasses, and weeds. The project uses daily-average category boundaries to provide Low, Moderate, High, and Very High messages. These can help with daily planning when the pollen category is known. An unclassified total count cannot simply use one category’s thresholds.

meteoswiss_pollen.name: MeteoSwiss pollen load classes
meteoswiss_pollen.description: MeteoSwiss pollen load classes distinguish specific types such as birch, grasses, and ragweed, with different concentration boundaries reflecting their allergenic potential. The project supports the types listed in the reference and shows their daily-average load class. This provides more context than a total count alone, but it is not a common EU standard or a prediction of an individual’s allergic reaction.
meteoswiss_pollen.organization: Swiss Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology

who_uv_index.name: WHO Global Solar UV Index
who_uv_index.description: The WHO Global Solar UV Index practical guide uses five exposure levels to explain the potential effects of solar UV on skin and eyes and help people plan sun protection and shade. The project adopts these levels and WHO’s specified RGB values for status and chart colors. Check whether a display shows the current index or the daily maximum; the UV Index is different from illuminance.
